barriers.description: The store-provided product database was incomplete, inconsistently labelled, and costly to revise, limiting the design team's ability to ensure accurate search results.
barriers.justification: Missing and mislabeled articles in the database prevented designers from achieving higher effectiveness in the search engine and constrained iterative usability improvements and valid evaluation of the interface.
barriers.reference_excerpt: This database consists of more than 60,000 different products, sometimes with several variations... Many terms and definitions did not conform with everyday language use. Further, not every article was included with its actual location.

barriers.description: The mobile robot was often unavailable for user testing because of intensive technical system revisions, forcing evaluations to be run on a stationary terminal instead.
barriers.justification: Lack of access to the mobile robot impeded designers' ability to evaluate and iterate the full embodied interaction and in-situ behaviors, limiting realistic usability testing and user understanding of the deployed system.
barriers.reference_excerpt: The user study was conducted at a stationary terminal and not with the mobile robot as it was seldom available due to intensive technical system revisions.

barriers.description: Faulty person-tracking and orientation caused the robot to lose sight of customers and collide with objects, disrupting interactions.
barriers.justification: Persistent tracking and orientation malfunctions interfered with smooth guidance tours and human-robot dialogs, preventing reliable evaluation of interaction flows and hindering iterative adaptation to user needs.
barriers.reference_excerpt: the robot began to move away when interested customers were moving towards it (11 %, n = 4). The main reason for this problem was the not perfectly working person-tracking function. This defect also affected the guidance tour to the article positions in the home improvement store.

barriers.description: Environmental noise, announcements, dialects and unclear speech made reliable speech recognition infeasible, forcing a shift to menu-based touch interactions.
barriers.justification: The noisy, variable store context prevented designers from implementing and evaluating speech-based interaction, constraining design options and requiring alternative interface solutions that changed the scope of user-centred exploration.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Speech recognition is significantly more complex than other typical human-computer interaction scenarios due to (i) the extreme background noise in home stores, (ii) distracting public address announcements, (iii) the large diversity of descriptions for the same article... Therefore, it proved to be unrealistic to use speech recognition in order to identify desired articles.

barriers.description: Customers were unwilling to wear RFID tags, making RFID-based user detection impracticable.
barriers.justification: User reluctance to carry tags removed a potential tracking solution, constraining designers' ability to facilitate and evaluate reliable user detection approaches and forcing reliance on other sensing modalities.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Moreover, RFID proved as not practicable for user detection and tracking, because most customers are not willing to wear RFID tags.

barriers.description: Data collection used overt observation and oral interviews, exposing the design team to social desirability and investigator effects that may bias findings.
barriers.justification: Potential social desirability and investigator effects reduce the validity of user insights and thereby constrain designers' ability to accurately manage user understanding and to reliably evaluate and iterate designs.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Data collection was partly conducted by overt observations and oral interviews. Therefore, social desirability and investigator effects cannot be excluded.

barriers.description: Hardware energy limitations (battery life) forced removal of nonverbal features (blinking) because they drained the battery and increased recharging frequency.
barriers.justification: Energy constraints prevented sustaining embodied nonverbal behaviors, limiting designers' ability to produce and evaluate holistic social interaction features and iterate on robot personality/presentation.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Initially, the robot blinked during oral interactions with customers. However, when it was used often, blinking drained the battery very fast, leading to frequent recharging. Therefore, that feature was turned off.

barriers.description: The store environment is large, maze-like and highly dynamic (people, carts, changing shelf layouts), making robust mapping and navigation difficult.
barriers.justification: Environmental complexity constrained designers' ability to produce and evaluate reliable navigation and context-of-use models, increasing technical difficulty and limiting straightforward iterative improvements.
barriers.reference_excerpt: TOOMAS was implemented in a home improvement store, which is a very complex, maze-like indoor environment... The environment is highly dynamic due to moving people (customers, staff) or other moving objects like shopping carts.
